lines: The class catalogue now comes from the backend, and the app keeps it on the device.
Seven classes, in order, each with its channel, focus, length and the rider level it opens at.
Every class has a YouTube video, a sync offset, a summary, a world, and a plan exactly as long as the class.
A class that breaks the rules is left out: a level outside one to thirty-two, a plan that does not add up, or a video id that is not YouTube's.
One class can be asked for by its id. An id the catalogue does not hold is not found, with a code to branch on.
The catalogue is public, so a rider can browse and start a solo class before signing in. Everything else still needs a session.
The catalogue is a file shipped inside the backend and read once. No table, no seed, and no test reads a file.
In the app, every catalogue the backend serves is kept on the device.
So when the backend cannot be reached, the class ride still finds its class, and the bike follows the plan.
The same ride, from a phone to a desktop, with no backend behind it.
What the tests prove: eight API tests, twelve rule cases, a new spec and six unit cases, all green.
Telo Ride, from the Telo family, turns a smart bike at home into a game.
It pairs with the bike over Bluetooth, reads your power and sets resistance for every hill and interval.

lines.text: Two doors: Race, ride a map against your best-time ghost, bots or people; and Classes, ride along to a video, alone or with a group; fed by one progression of XP, rider levels, stars and map unlocks.
